Derive

dih-RYVE — the root means 'stream'; to derive something is to draw it off, like water diverted from a stream. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To derive is to obtain something from a source, or to arise or stem from something.

Much of the region's income is thought to derive from its thriving tourism industry.

Worked Example

A small coastal town's entire economy traces back to a single decision a hundred years ago to build a lighthouse, which drew sailors, then merchants, then eventually the tourists who now support nearly every shop in town.

Tracing something back to its true origin or source is exactly what it means to derive it. Unlike 'invent,' which means to create something new, derive means to draw something from an existing source.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

trace (to): To trace something is to follow its trail step by step back to where it began -- tracing is the detective work of finding the path. To derive names the origin relationship itself: a thing can derive from a source whether or not anyone ever traces the path.

glean: To glean is to gather something bit by bit, with real effort, from scattered scraps and leftovers. To derive is more direct: you draw the thing you want from one identifiable source.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

originate: to be the very first source of something, rather than draw from one

invent: to create something entirely new

Where it sits · how closely it ties to a source — obtain → derive → stem (from)

obtain vs. derive: Obtain is more general than derive -- to obtain is simply to get hold of something that already exists, by any method at all, while derive specifically means to draw something out of an identifiable source.

stem (from) vs. derive: Stem from feels more natural and automatic than derive: results stem from their causes on their own, without anyone consciously drawing them out, while derive is usually a person's deliberate act.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — de-

prefix — de-: from, away (Latin)

root — -rive

root — -rive: stream (Latin (rivus))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin derivare meant 'to lead water away from a stream,' from de- ('from') and rivus ('stream'). To derive something, at its root, is to draw it off from its original source, the way a canal draws water from a river.

Use the root in a new word: rival

Use the root in a new word: rival: The two farms had been rivals for generations, ever since they first argued over water rights to the same river.
